stories.headline: Locked Himalayan fault raises concerns over major earthquake risk in Uttarakhand: Study
stories.title: Locked Himalayan fault raises concerns over major earthquake risk in Uttarakhand: Study
stories.summary: Satellite and ground-positioning data indicate that a 115-km-wide section of the Main Himalayan Thrust remains locked, raising concerns about long-term earthquake hazards in the central Himalayas
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A section of the tectonic plate named Main Himalayan Thrust beneath Uttarakhand is accumulating tectonic strain at a rate that researchers estimate could produce energy equivalent to a magnitude 8.1 earthquake over a century, according to a study presented at the European Geosciences Union (EGU) General Assembly 2026.

Titled Evidence of strong plate coupling in the Uttarakhand Himalayas: Constraints from GNSS and ALOS-2 InSAR observations, the study was conducted by Dibyashakti Panda, Mridul Yadav, Eric O. Lindsey and G Srinivasa Rao.
The researchers used ground-based satellite positioning measurements and radar imagery to investigate how the fault behaves as the Indian plate continues to move beneath the Himalayas.
The findings are significant because scientists have differed over how firmly the Main Himalayan Thrust (MHT) is locked beneath Uttarakhand.
The degree of locking helps determine how much tectonic movement is being stored as strain in the Earth’s crust rather than being released gradually through movement along the fault.
The researchers found that the fault remains locked across a width of approximately 115 km.
Their measurements indicate a slip deficit of around 18 millimetres a year, while satellite radar observations show peak ground uplift of 4–6 mm annually.

The findings point to a strongly coupled section of the fault, suggesting that the Indian plate’s continuing movement is not being accommodated through steady sliding across this portion of the megathrust.
Instead, the surrounding rocks are deforming as tectonic pressure accumulates.
What are the study’s major findings?
The researchers found that the Main Himalayan Thrust beneath Uttarakhand is strongly locked across a width of about 115 km.
A locked fault section is one where friction prevents the opposing sides from sliding freely, even as tectonic forces continue to push them against each other.

stories.headline: Virginia teen's model improves simulated earthquake sensor coverage by 16.7%
stories.title: Virginia teen's model improves simulated earthquake sensor coverage by 16.7%
stories.summary: A 14-year-old student from Williamsburg, Virginia, has become one of 30 finalists in a national science competition after developing a mathematical model to improve earthquake sensor placement. Isabel Rossi's six-month research project showed that adding just five sensors could increase simulated detection coverage by 16.7%. She used earthquake records from California and mathematical methods to identify better sensor locations.

stories.headline: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centres disrupt key services, derail AI research
stories.title: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centres disrupt key services, derail AI research
stories.summary: Moscow, Oct 22: Russia prides itself on its digital advances -- from an extensive e-commerce services sector to ambitious plans for developing artificial intelligence. But now, some of the key data centres at the heart of its technical prowess have been knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks in the 4.5-year-old full-scale invasion, suffering damage that could take a long time to repair. Ukraine this month hit three main data centres belonging to tech giant Yandex, one for Russia's biggest bank, Sberbank, and one for social media platform VKontakte, the country's equivalent to Facebook. While Yandex, Sberbank and VKontakte are coy about the damage, people and businesses across Russia have reported widespread interruptions to cloud services. Banking, e-commerce, geolocation and ride-hailing services, as well as Alisa, Yandex's virtual assistant, and multimodal AI chatbots all have suffered lasting disruptions. The fallout even spread to Russia's judicial system, reportedly forcing arbitration courts to cancel or postpone sessions and cutting database access. Most experts predict repairing the damage could take months, if not years. Some warn that Moscow's aspirations to become a leader in AI development could be significantly set back. “This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race,” said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Data centres have been hit by both sides in the war Data centres are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other's vital infrastructure. Russian missiles and drones have pummelled Ukraine's power grid and other key sites, part of Kremlin efforts to weaken morale and resistance. Moscow stepped up those attacks as winter approaches, taking advantage of a shortage of US-supplied Patriot interceptors, whose stockpiles have been drained by Washington's war with Iran. Ukraine retaliated with waves of drone attacks against Russian oil refineries, triggering a massive fuel crisis and bringing the war home to millions of civilians. US President Donald Trump has blamed the attacks for higher global oil prices, which have escalated largely due to the US war in Iran. Earlier this month, Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import diesel oil, shocking Ukraine and its allies. Ukraine also hit huge warehouses for Russia's top online retailers, Wildberries and Ozon. Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centres closely followed Moscow's recent strikes on data centres in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On October 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data centre in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A data centre in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck October 11. The data centre and AI hub for Sberbank was hit October 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data centre in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. Data centres are vulnerable While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centres are even softer targets -- massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives. The vulnerability of data centres was exposed by Iran, whose drones hit two Amazon Web Services data centres in the United Arab Emirates and one in Bahrain. AWS said last month it was unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted at two of them. Yandex has run drills for an accident that could incapacitate one of its six data centres, but it was caught unprepared when its three key facilities were hit over four days. It wasn't immediately clear why air defences near the sites had failed. “The problem in Russia is that they've got to cover a big country with air defence and they don't have enough,” said Nick Reiners, senior geotechnology analyst at Eurasia Group. Russia's efforts to build a sovereign internet backfire Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow's strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. “Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it's relatively easier to take down,” Reiners said. Klimarev predicted the data centre attacks could encourage many top Russian companies to move data abroad, while the authorities could ease their efforts to tighten internet controls to minimise the damage. “Paradoxically, the strikes on data centres have saved the Russian internet from isolation, as they will now have to move computing assets, most likely, to Europe,” Klimarev said. “It's quite likely that many Russian businesses are now roaming the European market to rent computing assets.” Russians are vexed by service disruptions Yandex dominates digital life in Russia and many former Soviet nations. It provides a wide variety of functions, including a search engine, cloud storage, payment apps, geolocation and ride-hailing services, and e-commerce platforms. “Yandex is kind of like Uber and Amazon and Google and everything rolled into one,” with everything "concentrated in just a few data centres,” Reiners said. “From a strategic perspective, they're an excellent target.” The attacks on Yandex caused unprecedented disruptions, paralysing payments, online orders, taxi rides and access to personal data. Moscow resident Igor Mann said he couldn't collect an order he placed with Yandex Market, an e-commerce platform. He said he tried using a virtual private network, but “nothing worked.” Taxi driver Pavel Belyavskiy, who gets orders via Yandex's ride-hailing app, couldn't connect with passengers. “On several orders already, I've ended up waiting for a long time and had to cancel the ride because I couldn't even get in touch with the passenger,” he said. The attacks also caused temporary disruptions at some major companies and banks that rely on Yandex cloud services. “It's not just about convenience -- it's also about work ... tied to everyday life,” said another Moscow resident, Eduard Malyavko. A blow to Russia's AI ambitions Yandex said it restored most key cloud services in the following days as it turned to other data centres in Russia. But the damage to the company's AI development efforts is widely seen as massive and longer-lasting. Yandex has invested in huge data centres as the global AI boom fuels demand for computing power. The company's three supercomputers used to develop models are ranked among the top 500 in the world. Its most powerful computer -- at the Sasovo data centre -- was ranked 19th. Yandex didn't disclose the extent of the strikes' consequences, but satellite images indicated its data centres sustained serious damage. Some observers noted that fires triggered by the attacks probably seriously damaged high-end chips and other key equipment. “With this kind of hit, it's hard to expect that at least something was left intact -- the data centres' equipment is fragile, demanding and expensive,” Klimarev said. “Soot from the fire is bad for electronics.” While Russia already lagged years behind the US and China, “Ukraine's drone strikes will likely still set back Russian AI efforts further,” said Connor Martin, an expert with the Council for Foreign Relations. He said in a commentary that Russia likely will struggle to quickly replace the US-designed Nvidia A100 chips powering Yandex's supercomputers. Klimarev also said the global deficit of high-end chips, combined with the sanctions on their delivery to Russia, will make repairs long and costly. “I'm not sure it can be done in half a year, a year, or even at all,” he said.

stories.headline: HP High Court Refuses To Reject Suit Challenging Cooperative Society Election, Says Defence Cannot Be Considered Under Order VII Rule 11 CPC
stories.title: HP High Court Refuses To Reject Suit Challenging Cooperative Society Election, Says Defence Cannot Be Considered Under Order VII Rule 11 CPC
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The Himachal Pradesh High Court has reiterated that while deciding an application for rejection of a plaint under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, courts must confine their examination to the averments in the plaint and the documents accompanying it, without considering the defence raised by the defendants.

Dismissing a petition challenging the rejection of such an application in a dispute overthe election of a cooperative society's managing committee, the Court held that the trial court had rightly refused to reject the plaint at this stage.
The case arose from a dispute over the August 25, 2023 election of the managing committee of the Katohar Khurd Cooperative Agriculture Service Society in Una, Himachal Pradesh.
The plaintiffs alleged that their nomination forms had been illegally rejected and that the election process was conducted in violation of the prescribed rules.
They sought to declare the election null and void and requested the appointment of an administrator until fresh elections were held.
The defendants sought rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 CPC, arguing that the suit was barred under Sections 72 and 76 of the Himachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act, 1968.
After the trial court dismissed their application, the defendants approached the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution.
The High Court observed that an application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC must be decided solely on the basis of the plaint and accompanying documents, without considering the defendants' defence.

It held that the plaintiffs' contention regarding the delay in adjudication of the election dispute under Section 72 of the Himachal Pradesh Cooperative Societies Act, 1968, had been rightly considered by the trial court.
The Court further noted that a plaint cannot be partially rejected when multiple reliefs are sought and the suit cannot be rejected in its entirety.

Finding no grounds to interfere with the trial court's order under Article 227 of the Constitution, the High Court dismissed the petition, clarifying that its observations would not affect the merits of the underlying suit.

stories.headline: Udhayanidhi says election petition against him was filed in Madras High Court after 45-day mark
stories.title: Udhayanidhi says election petition against him was filed in Madras High Court after 45-day mark
stories.summary: Justice G. Arul Murugan winds up hearing oral arguments on applications filed by the Leader of the Opposition to reject the election petition and strike off pleadings
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Tamil Nadu’s Leader of the Opposition (LoP) Udhayanidhi Stalin has contended before the Madras High Court that an election petition challenging his victory from the Chepauk-Thiruvallikeni Assembly constituency in the 2026 polls has been filed after the expiry of the statutory time limit of 45 days.

Appearing before Justice G. Arul Murugan, senior counsel P. Wilson urged the judge to reject the election petition at the threshold, without taking it up for trial, on the ground that it had been filed after the limitation period, prescribed under Section 81 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, ended.
The counsel said, the LoP had secured 62,992 votes as against his nearest rival candidate D. Selvam of the TVK, who got 55,852 votes.
The election petition had been filed by P. Milany of Theni district, who had also contested from the Chepauk-Thiruvallikeni constituency and secured 30 votes.
Highlighting that Mr. Udhayanidhi was declared elected on May 4, 2026, the counsel claimed the election petition challenging his victory ought to have been filed on or before June 17, 2026.
Since the present petition had been filed on June 18, 2026, he argued it was barred by limitation.
The counsel contended that the principle of excluding the first day, under the General Clauses Act of 1897, for the purpose of calculating limitation period would not apply to election petitions.
He underlined that Section 81 of the 1951 Act specifically uses the term “from the date of election of the returned candidate.”
“Normally, MiLord, Your Lordship knows that if a judgment is pronounced today, the limitation would begin only from the next day.
But the 1951 Act is a special legislation and it specifically states that an election petition must be presented within 45 days from the date of the election of the returned candidate,” he said.

The counsel said, the Election Commission of India (ECI) had also sent a communication to the Registrar General of the High Court confirming that the election petitions with respect to the 2026 general elections must be filed in the High Court on or before June 17, 2026.

He relied upon a Supreme Court judgment in Youaraj Rai versus Chander Bahadur (2006) and argued that the top court, too, had categorically held that the limitation period for filing an election petition would begin from the date of election of the returned candidate.

stories.headline: Iran’s IRGC says 4 ships hit, set ablaze in Gulf; 3 others strike mines near Hormuz
stories.title: Iran’s IRGC says 4 ships hit, set ablaze in Gulf; 3 others strike mines near Hormuz
stories.summary: Tehran , October 22: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has claimed that it struck and set fire to four ships carrying oil cargoes in the northern Persian Gulf, while three other vessels collided with mines in the western Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian state media, Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB). In a statement issued on Thursday, the IRGC Navy said the four ships had previously crossed an “illegal route” despite warnings to the maritime companies operating them. “Following previous warnings to the offending maritime companies, who had been deceived by the invading US military and had crossed illegal routes, Navy fighters, by observing and pursuing four offending ships, which had previously crossed the illegal route, discovered them transferring oil cargoes in the middle of the northern Persian Gulf, where all four ships were hit simultaneously and caught fire,” the statement said, as reported by IRIB. The IRGC Navy also claimed that three other vessels had struck mines in the western Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday night and were stopped. The statement came amid heightened tensions over maritime movement through the strategically important waterway, through which a significant share of global oil shipments passes. Reiterating its control over the strait, the IRGC Navy said its personnel continued to manage maritime movement with the support of the Iranian public. “With this enormous national support, the IRGC Navy sailors continue to manage and control the Strait of Hormuz,” the statement said. The Iranian force also blamed the United States for the reported maritime incidents, accusing Washington of encouraging vessels to navigate through "illegally mined passage". "The insistence of the arrogant US regime on inciting ships to pass through the illegally mined passage has increased maritime incidents day by day," the statement said. Issuing a warning to Washington, the IRGC Navy said the confrontation could expand if the situation continued. "The aggressive US army should know that if this trend continues, the scope of the confrontation will be extended to the aggressive bases in the region. This is a serious warning," it added. The statement did not identify the vessels involved or provide details about their ownership, the extent of the reported damage or any casualties. The claim of strikes on the ships came as US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said that the United States is not negotiating with Iran and "something" will happen "fairly soon." Speaking to American news network NewsNation 's White House correspondent Libbey Dean, Trump was asked about developments in negotiations with Tehran; Trump initially acknowledged some activity but indicated that the outcome remained uncertain. “A little bit, but we'll see what happens,” Trump said when asked whether negotiations with Iran were ongoing. Asked whether he was done negotiating with the Iranian government, Trump said, "No, I think we're not negotiating...we are going to have something, one way or the other. It'll happen fairly soon." In the interview, Trump also highlighted the situation between Washington and Tehran as "a little conflict against Iran" and said the United States was performing well on both military and economic fronts. "I think our sanctions ended the real deal over there. But we're doing very well militarily and financially against Iran," he said. Citing US officials and other people briefed on the deliberations, the report said the two militaries have stepped up exercises, including flying aircraft over Iraq to practise strike manoeuvres. Amid the possibility of renewed strikes, Iran has warned that it would respond to any renewed military action. According to Iranian state-affiliated media outlet Student News Network (SNN), IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said, "The United States has the ‘Mother of All Bombs.’ We will show them the ‘Father of All Bombs,’ and it will definitely be something new for them." But Tehran has not provided details about the weapon or clarified what the threat entails. The warning follows reports that US President Donald Trump has considered using the 22,000-pound GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB), known as the "Mother of All Bombs", against Iran’s deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility. According to The New York Times, the United States is assembling a substantial military force expected to be fully in place by early November, including three aircraft carriers, thousands of Marines, fighter jets and Special Operations forces. Officials have cited political considerations, including Trump’s earlier pledge not to strike Iran before the midterm elections, as reasons the operation could be delayed. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, has highlighted the situation as a major challenge for Tehran. In an address to the Iranian Parliament, Pezeshkian said, "The memorandum of understanding we signed was very good; we hadn't given anything. The current situation is neither good for us, nor for the region, nor for the world." He added, "We are in a super-challenge, not a challenge. America didn't think we would stand firm despite the pressure and war, but we stood firm, and we will continue to stand firm." The New York Times report said Washington was seeking to use the prospect of renewed military action as leverage in negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme and control over the Strait of Hormuz. However, Iranian negotiators have resisted making concessions on the nuclear issue, insisting that the matter be deferred until later in the talks. As military preparations and diplomatic efforts continue, the possibility of renewed strikes has raised concerns about a wider regional conflict, with uncertainty persisting over Trump’s final decision and Iran’s potential response. stories.headline: Iran says 7 tankers were damaged in Strait of Hormuz
stories.title: Iran says 7 tankers were damaged in Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: Dubai, Oct 22: Iran's state television reported that seven oil tankers were either struck by attacks or hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight Thursday, possibly the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the Iran war started on February 28. Here is the latest news from the Middle East. Read our full coverage here. 7 oil tankers damaged in Strait of Hormuz, Iran's state television reports ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Iran's state television reported that seven oil tankers caught fire and were damaged overnight Thursday after being targeted or striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. If verified, it would be the largest single-day number of vessels damaged in the waterway since the start of the Iran war on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran. Quoting a statement by the Revolutionary Guard's navy, the Iranian report said that four of the tankers were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire. Another three were damaged and immobilised when they hit naval mines. The report didn't provide details about possible casualties or the flags of the tankers. The report also warned that the Revolutionary Guard may target US bases in the region if the US tried to allow oil tankers to transit through other parts of the strait. The Revolutionary Guard had routinely targeted US bases in Gulf countries during the war. Yemen's government warns Houthi rallies could be targeted ---------------------------------------------------------------- Yemen's Defence Ministry said Thursday that Houthi rallies and mobilisation programmes will be considered legitimate military targets and warned residents in Houthi-held areas against taking part. The announcement was shared in a social media post and is considered a major escalation against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as civilians living in areas under their control. Deliberate attacks on civilians could amount to a war crime. Rallies and what Houthis call “cultural courses” are one of the Iranian-backed group's main tools for mobilisation of supporters and fighters. The Defence Ministry statement said such assemblies are used by the Houthis to mobilise children for combat. Death toll from strike on Saudi airport rises to 2 --------------------------------------------------- Saudi Arabia's Civil Aviation Authority said Thursday that the number of people killed in an attack on the King Fahd International Airport has risen to two. The dead are a Saudi citizen and an Indian national who was living in the kingdom, according to a statement. Another eight people suffered injuries in the attack that occurred late Wednesday. Saudi authorities didn't say who was responsible for the attack or provide any details about the attack reported earlier Thursday. The Houthi rebels issued no statement. King Fahd Airport on the country's east near Bahrain and Qatar has been attacked previously amid a wider wave of Houthi missile and projectile strikes targeting major airports in Saudi Arabia. Disabled Syrian man killed in Israeli forces raid ------------------------------------------------- A civilian with special needs was killed during an Israeli forces raid Thursday on the village of Jamla in southern Syria's Daraa province, Syrian state news agency SANA reported. It did not give more details about how the disabled man was killed. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment. After the ouster of former Syrian President Bashar Assad in a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024, Israel seized control of a UN-patrolled buffer zone in southern Syria and has occupied it since. Jamla isn't inside the Israeli occupied zone but Israeli forces often make incursions into areas outside the zone. (AP)

stories.headline: Indian-American Ramaswamy defends attack ad against rival Acton
stories.title: Indian-American Ramaswamy defends attack ad against rival Acton
stories.summary: Washington, Oct 22 : Indian-American Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign for Ohio governor is standing by a one-minute attack ad in which Democratic rival Amy Acton’s estranged birth mother calls her “a liar”, even as Vice President J.D. Vance rallied voters for him in suburban Cincinnati. The Ramaswamy campaign confirmed late on Tuesday that it had produced the ad featuring Donna Arthur, Acton’s birth mother, according to Axios and The Hill. Campaign spokesperson Connie Luck said Arthur was not paid and that the campaign would spend $4 million promoting the ad online and on television, the reports said. Acton has said she was removed from her mother at the age of 12 “for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse,” according to reports by The Hill and WOUB. The ad drew sharp criticism. Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown called it “disgusting”, while commentator Meghan McCain described it as “dastardly”, the reports said. Casey Putsch, a former Republican rival of Ramaswamy, said he would vote for Acton. PolitiFact, which examined the ad’s claims on Wednesday, reviewed the dispute between Acton and her birth mother over her childhood. At a rally with Vance in Sharonville on Wednesday, Ramaswamy did not mention Acton at all, according to the Dayton Daily News. Instead, he pitched his plans for zero state income tax, lower electricity bills, property-tax cuts and support for the steel industry, the paper reported. Vance, however, defended the ad, saying the campaign “told it like it is”, according to public radio stations WYSO and WVXU. A heckler was removed from the event, the stations reported. On X, Ramaswamy accused Acton of “hiding from debate” and said she “bans cameras” at her events. He also posted a video titled “A strong message to Republicans” and shared a segment by broadcaster Megyn Kelly on Acton. The timing is significant. More than 676,000 Ohioans have already cast their ballots, according to the reports. A recent Marist poll has closely tracked the race. Former President Barack Obama is due to join Brown and Acton at a rally in Cleveland on October 24, WYSO reported, in a sign that Democrats see the governor’s race as competitive in a state that has trended Republican. Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur born in Cincinnati to immigrant parents from Kerala, ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024 before endorsing Donald Trump. He briefly co-led the Department of Government Efficiency effort with Elon Musk before launching his bid for governor. Acton, a physician, served as director of the Ohio Department of Health during the early months of the Covid-19 pandemic. Ohio votes in the November 3 general election. --IANS

stories.headline: Supreme Court to hear Ashish Mishra plea in Lakhimpur Kheri case
stories.title: Supreme Court to hear Ashish Mishra plea in Lakhimpur Kheri case
stories.summary: Supreme Court to hear Ashish Mishra plea in Lakhimpur Kheri case
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: The Supreme Court is likely to hear Ashish Mishra's plea on October 26.
The hearing comes as the trial nears completion and judicial conduct faces scrutiny.

The Supreme Court is likely to hear on October 26 a plea linked to the 2021 Lakhimpur Kheri violence case, in which eight people were killed during a farmers' protest, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The court had directed the Uttar Pradesh government to appoint a new public prosecutor for the trial.
On October 5, it also asked the Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court to act quickly on allegations that the presiding officer had transferred several cases to himself and acquitted the accused.

According to the Supreme Court website, a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana will take up a plea filed by Ashish Mishra, the son of former Union minister Ajay Mishra 'Teni' and the prime accused in the case.
Mishra had approached the Supreme Court seeking bail and, after securing it, sought relaxation of the bail conditions.
On August 6, the court refused to relax the conditions further.
The violence took place on October 3, 2021, at Tikunia in Uttar Pradesh's Lakhimpur Kheri district during a protest against Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya's visit to the area.
Four farmers were run over by an SUV.
A driver and two BJP workers were then allegedly lynched by angry farmers, while a journalist also died in the violence.
The trial is nearing completion, with the trial court having examined 86 of the 130 prosecution witnesses, PTI reported.

stories.headline: Should India be concerned about Pakistan's new Badr defence deal?
stories.title: Should India be concerned about Pakistan's new Badr defence deal?
stories.summary: Should India be concerned about Pakistan's new Badr defence deal?
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'defence deal' in title weight 44
event term: 'defence deal' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: Pakistan has signed an MoU with Turkiye, Qatar and Indonesia to deepen cooperation in defence production, months after the Mecca pact.
Will it impact India, considering its existing defence agreements with Indonesia?
Another Islamic defence axis may be taking shape, with Pakistan signing an MoU with Turkiye, Qatar and Indonesia to deepen cooperation in defence production and bolster military capabilities.
Signed in Doha with little fanfare, the Badr agreement, unlike the Mecca pact, is not a promise to fight together, but a plan to build defence capabilities together.

For India, it raises two concerns: Pakistan's efforts to diversify its sources of weapons and military technology, and Indonesia's participation, coming months after signing a deal with New Delhi for BrahMos missiles.
While details of the memorandum are scant, it mostly focuses on joint defence manufacturing, technology sharing, military training and research and development among the four countries.
Essentially, it mostly concerns industrial cooperation rather than a mutual defence pledge.
Turkiye, in fact, already has military manufacturing ties with Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia separately.
What the Badr MoU does is closely integrate the supply chains of the countries.
Each country brings its own set of resources and skills.
While Turkiye boasts one of the world's most advanced defence sectors, Pakistan and Indonesia offer manufacturing capacity and labour.
Qatar, on the other hand, brings investment and demand.

stories.title: Jio Platforms IPO: Gaurang Shah Recommends Subscription, Cites Long-Term Growth And Tariff Hikes
stories.summary: Jio Platforms’ IPO has drawn strong investor demand, with subscriptions surging on the opening day. Gaurang Shah, Senior Vice President, Geojit Investments, shares his outlook on the IPO, highlighting the company’s massive subscriber base, telecom sector resilience and potential tariff hikes as key long-term growth drivers. Higher average revenue per user (ARPU) could support revenue growth, while Jio’s decade-long expansion strengthens its position in India’s digital economy. Shah advises investors to look beyond listing gains and focus on long-term wealth creation. He also discloses that Geojit Investments has issued a subscribe recommendation for the IPO.

stories.headline: RBI MPC minutes show economists sticking to back-to-back rate hikes
stories.title: RBI MPC minutes show economists sticking to back-to-back rate hikes
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 22 : Economists on Thursday maintained back-to-back repo rate hike stance, as the RBI MPC minutes for October revealed more hawkish tone, inclining towards future risk and policy tightening. A report by SBI Research said that it continues to maintain 50 bps rate hike in December, either through a “plain vanila” 50 bps repo rate hike or an “exotic” 50 bps rate hike with a 25-bps repo rate and a 25-bps asymmetric widening of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor (MSF at 6.25 per cent and SDF at 5.50 per cent). “The broadening of inflationary pressures, alongside persistent rupee weakness, calls for close monitoring by the RBI and a calibrated policy response to contain inflation risks and reinforce monetary transmission,” said Dr Soumya Kanti Ghosh, Group Chief Economic Adviser, State Bank of India. “We expect the peak inflation rate by November below 6.5 per cent and with these elevated levels, such generalisation warrants close monitoring by the RBI,” Dr Ghosh added. According to Radhika Rao, Senior Economist and Executive Director, DBS Bank, the minutes from the RBI’s October rate meeting reflected the hawkish pivot, where the repo rate was raised by 25 bp and stance was changed to ‘calibrated tightening’. “Members cited rising inflationary pressures and firm growth as reasons behind the 25bp hike. Tone of the commentary put two external members in the most hawkish camp, as they emphasised the broadening inflation risks and need for pre-emptive action, while two others were considered mildly hawkish/neutral as they supported only incremental hikes and explicitly rejected signalling a prolonged tightening cycle,” she explained. The RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra highlighted emerging signs of inflation becoming more generalised. With inflation set to rise to 6 per cent in CY Q4, “the door remains open for a back-to-back hike in December,” said Rao. In markets, bond yields stayed high, while the rupee was appreciated due to forex regulatory measures. As restrictions gained traction, the rupee has strengthened by around 1.5 per cent/USD this month, defying the usual headwinds from rising oil prices and subdued global risk sentiment, while FX forward premiums remain elevated. Inflows towards the country’s biggest-ever equity IPO also contributed to forex gains, said economists. For now, the currency is exhibiting limited reaction to external developments, while bonds are set to remain under pressure as oil supply fears return to the table, said Rao. --IANS

stories.headline: TPCI, UKIBC sign pact to boost India-UK trade ties
stories.title: TPCI, UKIBC sign pact to boost India-UK trade ties
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 22 : The Trade Promotion Council of India (TPCI) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the UK-India Business Council (UKIBC) to deepen bilateral commercial ties following the entry into force of the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), it was announced on Thursday. The MoU between TPCI and UKIBC establishes a framework for institutional business collaboration. The partnership focuses on connecting businesses, facilitating trade missions, sharing market intelligence, and creating growth opportunities for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) across both nations, according to a TPCI statement. In tandem with the MoU signing, TPCI also organised a B2B matchmaking showcase in London featuring 48 Indian exporting companies and 150 UK-based importers. The food and beverage sector represents a significant growth corridor under the new trade framework. Notably, the UK currently imports $50.68 billion worth of processed food annually with India's share at 0.6 per cent ($309.5 million), presenting significant room for expansion. Under CETA, UK tariffs of up to 70 per cent on processed foods, 4.2-8.5 per cent on shrimp, and duties on instant coffee have been eliminated. Mohit Singla, Chairman, TPCI, said, “This MoU is a major milestone in taking India-UK trade engagement from policy to partnership. Following the entry into force of the India-UK CETA, both TPCI and UKIBC will be deeply engaged in bilateral trade development, ensuring that the post-FTA momentum translates into tangible outcomes.” Singla further stated that with 99 per cent of Indian tariff lines now entering the UK duty-free, and peak tariffs of up to 70 per cent on processed foods eliminated under CETA, the landscape for Indian food exporters has transformed dramatically.” Apart from that, the TPCI team also held meetings with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), London Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) and the Scotch Whisky Association. “Both sides discussed business support while boosting international trade to drive economic growth,” according to TPCI. Moreover, bilateral trade between India and the UK reached 48 billion pounds ($65 billion) in FY2025-26. After this, Indian food exporters are poised to scale exports, expand beyond the 1.86 million Indian diaspora market and establish supply chains across UK retail and food service sectors. --IANS
